title: Identity Security Training Path
subtitle: A staged, self-paced course through authentication, authorization, identity lifecycle, and the systems around them. Read the lesson, explore the linked diagram, then pass the stage quiz.

stages.title: Foundations
stages.summary: The vocabulary and mental models everything else builds on: identity vs. authentication vs. authorization, sessions, and how to read the diagrams in this repository.

lessons.title: Identity, authentication, and authorization
lessons.objective: Tell apart the three ideas people most often conflate.
lessons.content:
Three distinct questions sit at the heart of every access decision:

Identity — who are you? A claim to be a particular principal (a person, a service, a device). An identifier like a username or a sub claim names the identity; it is not proof.

Authentication (authN) — can you prove it? Verifying the claim with one or more factors: something you know (password), have (a passkey, a token), or are (biometric). The output is a trusted assertion that this principal is present.

Authorization (authZ) — what are you allowed to do? Given a proven identity, deciding whether a specific action on a specific resource is permitted. Roles, attributes, relationships, and policy live here.

The order matters: you authenticate first to establish who, then authorize to decide what. A system can authenticate you perfectly and still deny you — that is authorization doing its job.

lessons.title: How to read the diagrams
lessons.objective: Get fluent in the three views every flow uses.
lessons.content:
Most flows in this library are drawn three ways, and each answers a different question:

Sequence — the messages exchanged over time, in order. Best for “what actually goes over the wire, and in what order?”

Swimlane — the same flow with one lane per actor (User, Browser, IdP, API…). Best for “who is responsible for each step?”

Flowchart — the decision and error logic, with every deny/error path drawn explicitly. Best for “where can this fail, and what gates each outcome?”

Each flow folder also carries a Status badge — ✅ Current, 🟡 Legacy, ⛔ Deprecated, 🔵 Emerging — so you can tell at a glance whether a mechanism is something to build on or something to migrate off.

lessons.title: Sessions and tokens
lessons.objective: Understand how a system remembers you after you authenticate.
lessons.content:
Authentication happens once, but you make many requests. Something has to carry the “I already proved who I am” signal on each one. Two broad approaches:

Server-side session — the server stores session state and hands the browser an opaque session cookie. Each request sends the cookie; the server looks up the session. Easy to revoke (delete the session), but the server holds state.

Token — the client holds a signed token (often a JWT) that carries claims the server can verify without a lookup. Stateless and scalable, but harder to revoke before expiry — which is why short lifetimes, refresh rotation, and mechanisms like introspection and CAE exist.

The interactive Flow Explorer lets you step through a real token flow and see exactly what each request carries.

quiz.q: A user signs in successfully but gets a 403 when opening the admin page. Which stage denied them?
choices: Authentication
Authorization
Identity resolution
Session creation
quiz.explain: They proved who they are (authentication succeeded); the system then decided this proven identity may not perform this action — that is authorization.

quiz.q: You want to know exactly which HTTP requests a flow makes and in what order. Which diagram view is best?
choices: Swimlane
Flowchart
Sequence
Status badge
quiz.explain: The sequence diagram shows the ordered messages exchanged over time. Swimlane shows responsibilities; flowchart shows decision/error logic.

quiz.q: Which statement about server-side sessions vs. tokens is correct?
choices: Tokens are always more secure than sessions
Server-side sessions are easy to revoke; stateless tokens are harder to revoke before they expire
Session cookies cannot be used with HTTPS
JWTs are stored on the server, not the client
quiz.explain: Deleting a server-side session revokes it immediately. A stateless JWT stays valid until it expires, which is why short lifetimes, refresh rotation, introspection, and CAE exist.

quiz.q: A diagram carries a ⛔ Deprecated status badge. What does that signal?
choices: It is the newest, recommended approach
It is actively discouraged; prefer the linked alternative
It is still the default for new builds
It has not been reviewed yet
quiz.explain: ⛔ Deprecated means the mechanism is discouraged for new work and the page points to what to use instead (e.g. the OIDC Implicit flow → Authorization Code + PKCE).

stages.title: Web SSO: OIDC & SAML
stages.summary: The two protocols that carry single sign-on across the web: OpenID Connect (the modern default) and SAML 2.0 (the enterprise incumbent). How each moves a proven identity from an IdP to an app, and how to pick between them.

lessons.title: OIDC Authorization Code + PKCE
lessons.objective: Explain why PKCE is the modern default for SPAs and native apps, and what the verifier actually protects.
lessons.content:
The Authorization Code flow with PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange, RFC 7636) is the current recommended flow for public clients — single-page apps and native/mobile apps that cannot keep a client secret. The app never holds a secret, so a stolen authorization code alone must not be redeemable.

PKCE closes that gap. Before redirecting to /authorize, the app generates a random code_verifier (43–128 chars, kept only in memory) and sends its hash: code_challenge = BASE64URL(SHA256(code_verifier)) with code_challenge_method=S256. When it later redeems the code at /token, it presents the original code_verifier. The IdP recomputes the hash and rejects any mismatch with invalid_grant. An attacker who intercepts the redirect gets a code but never the verifier, so the code is useless.

PKCE stops code interception — it does not replace state (CSRF binding) or nonce (ID-token replay binding), both still required. Use S256, never plain: with plain the challenge equals the verifier, so anyone who saw the /authorize request already has it. Current security guidance recommends PKCE for all clients, confidential ones included, as extra code-injection defense.

Step through it end to end in the Flow Explorer to see exactly what each request carries.

lessons.title: OIDC Authorization Code for confidential clients
lessons.objective: Trace how a server-side app redeems a code over the back channel so tokens never touch the browser.
lessons.content:
The baseline OpenID Connect flow is built for a confidential client — a server-side web app with a backend that can hold credentials. The browser is redirected to /authorize with response_type=code&scope=openid; the user authenticates and consents; the IdP returns a short-lived, single-use authorization code through the browser (the front channel).

The important part happens next, out of the browser's reach: the backend redeems the code at the /token endpoint over a direct back-channel HTTPS call, authenticating itself with client_secret_basic or the stronger private_key_jwt. It receives an ID token, an access token, and optionally a refresh token. Tokens never transit the browser, which is the security advantage over front-channel token delivery.

The client then validates the ID token: signature against the IdP's JWKS, iss, aud equal to its client_id, exp, and a nonce match. It must also verify state on the callback before touching the code (a mismatch is treated as CSRF and discarded). Codes are single-use and short-lived; the IdP detects reuse and revokes any tokens already issued for that code. Register an exact-match redirect_uri — no wildcards, no open redirectors.

Prefer private_key_jwt where supported: it avoids a shared secret and enables key rotation. A public client uses this same flow plus PKCE.

lessons.title: SAML SP-initiated SSO
lessons.objective: Walk the AuthnRequest-to-assertion exchange and name the checks the SP must perform.
lessons.content:
SAML 2.0 is the enterprise incumbent for workforce SSO, and SP-initiated Web Browser SSO is its canonical flow. The user starts at the application — the Service Provider (SP) — which builds an AuthnRequest and sends it to the Identity Provider (IdP) via the HTTP-Redirect binding: the request is DEFLATE-compressed, base64- and URL-encoded into the SAMLRequest query parameter. RelayState carries the deep link the user originally wanted so the SP can restore it after login.

The IdP authenticates the user (or reuses an existing IdP session for seamless SSO) and returns a signed Response containing an Assertion. It is delivered as a base64 SAMLResponse form field auto-posted to the SP's Assertion Consumer Service (ACS) URL via the HTTP-POST binding.

The SP's validation is where security lives: verify the XML signature before trusting any content, using the IdP certificate from metadata (never one embedded in the message alone). Then check Issuer, Destination, the Audience restriction, the NotBefore/NotOnOrAfter conditions, and SubjectConfirmationData — including InResponseTo, which must match a request ID the SP actually issued. Enforce one-time use of the assertion ID (a replay cache), and guard against XML Signature Wrapping by consuming only the element the signature truly covers. Treat RelayState as untrusted input and allow-list it to prevent open redirects.

Because the SP originated the request, it controls InResponseTo correlation and can demand fresh auth with ForceAuthn="true" — which is why SP-initiated is preferred over IdP-initiated SSO, where an unsolicited response has no InResponseTo to correlate.

lessons.title: Choosing SAML vs OIDC
lessons.objective: Decide which protocol a given app should use, and justify it in one line.
lessons.content:
Both protocols achieve federated SSO — a trusted IdP proves identity and hands the result to an app — but they differ in shape and era. OIDC is JSON/JWT over OAuth 2.0, with broad library support and first-class fits for SPAs, native/mobile, and API-fronted apps. SAML 2.0 is XML with redirect/POST bindings: verbose, but ubiquitous in enterprise IdPs (Okta, Entra ID, ADFS, Shibboleth) and partner federations.

The default rule: greenfield browser and mobile apps should choose OIDC. SAML is marked 🟡 Legacy for new consumer/greenfield apps — not a runtime warning; SAML remains valid and widely deployed. Keep SAML where an existing enterprise IdP or partner already speaks it, which is common in workforce SSO. SAML also has no clean native/mobile or SPA story, so those cases point firmly to OIDC.

Note the two protocols are not the whole map: domain-joined intranet Windows apps may be better served by Kerberos, and pure service-to-service or single-first-party-app cases may need no federation at all (mutual TLS, an API key, or a plain session cookie). Picking OIDC is also only half the decision — you then choose the right OAuth grant (Authorization Code + PKCE for public clients).

Work the decision top-down with the protocol decision guide, then confirm the tradeoffs in its comparison table before committing.

quiz.q: In the OIDC Authorization Code + PKCE flow, what does the code_verifier protect against?
choices: An attacker who intercepts the authorization code redeeming it, because they lack the verifier
CSRF on the authorization request
Replay of the ID token
The IdP's TLS certificate being spoofed
quiz.explain: PKCE binds the code to a secret held only in the app. A stolen code is useless without the code_verifier, which the IdP re-hashes and checks at /token. CSRF is handled by state and ID-token replay by nonce — both still required alongside PKCE.

quiz.q: Why should PKCE use code_challenge_method=S256 rather than plain?
choices: plain is faster but produces a longer challenge
With plain the challenge equals the verifier, so anyone who saw the /authorize request already has the secret
plain does not work over HTTPS
S256 lets the app skip sending state and nonce
quiz.explain: plain sends the verifier itself as the challenge, so an interceptor of the /authorize request learns it and PKCE gives no protection. S256 sends only the SHA-256 hash. S256 does not remove the need for state or nonce.

quiz.q: What is the defining advantage of the confidential-client Authorization Code flow's back-channel token exchange?
choices: It skips the /authorize redirect entirely
Tokens are returned directly in the browser URL for speed
Tokens never transit the browser — the code is redeemed server-to-server at /token
It removes the need to validate the ID token signature
quiz.explain: Only a single-use code goes through the front channel (browser); the backend redeems it over a direct HTTPS call, authenticating with a secret or private_key_jwt, so tokens never reach the browser. The ID token must still be validated (iss, aud, exp, nonce, signature).

quiz.q: In SAML SP-initiated SSO, which SP-side check specifically defends against unsolicited or attacker-injected responses?
choices: DEFLATE-compressing the SAMLRequest
Matching InResponseTo against a request ID the SP actually issued
Storing RelayState server-side
Using the HTTP-POST binding for the response
quiz.explain: InResponseTo ties the response to a pending AuthnRequest the SP originated, so a response the SP never asked for is rejected. This correlation is exactly what IdP-initiated SSO lacks, which is why SP-initiated is preferred. RelayState storage and bindings are transport concerns, not injection defenses.

quiz.q: A team is building a brand-new mobile app and a partner already runs a corporate SAML IdP for its internal web portal. What does the decision guide recommend?
choices: Use SAML for both, since the IdP already speaks it
OIDC (Authorization Code + PKCE) for the new mobile app; keep SAML for the existing enterprise portal
Use OIDC for both and decommission the SAML IdP immediately
Use Kerberos for the mobile app
quiz.explain: Greenfield browser/mobile apps default to OIDC — SAML has no clean native/mobile story and is 🟡 Legacy for new apps. But SAML stays valid where an enterprise IdP already uses it, so keep the existing portal on SAML rather than forcing a migration. Kerberos is for domain-joined intranet apps, not internet mobile clients.

stages.title: Tokens, sessions & logout
stages.summary: How an authenticated session is kept alive, validated, and torn down: refresh-token rotation with reuse detection, introspection vs. local JWT validation and revocation, the three OIDC logout mechanisms, and how to choose a session representation without reaching for deprecated flows.

lessons.title: Refresh tokens & rotation with reuse detection
lessons.objective: Renew access without re-prompting the user, and detect a stolen refresh token.
lessons.content:
Access tokens are deliberately short-lived, but users stay signed in far longer. A refresh token bridges the gap: the client presents it at the token endpoint with grant_type=refresh_token and receives a fresh access token — no user interaction. For OIDC the client asks for this capability with the offline_access scope, subject to consent.

Rotation hardens this. On each refresh the authorization server issues a new refresh token and invalidates the old one. Public clients (SPAs, native apps) must rotate; confidential clients should, or sender-constrain instead.

Rotation is what makes reuse detection possible. Once a refresh token has been rotated away, it should never be seen again. If an already-used token is presented, two parties hold copies — one of them is a thief. The AS cannot tell which, so it revokes the entire token family and forces interactive re-authentication. Every reuse trip is a probable theft: log and alert on it.

Two expiry models bound the family: sliding expiry extends an idle window on each refresh, while absolute expiry sets a hard ceiling from initial authorization. Robust deployments combine them — a sliding idle timeout capped by an absolute lifetime. On refresh you may narrow scope with the scope parameter, never widen it. Errors surface as invalid_grant (expired, revoked, reused, or unknown token).

lessons.title: Validating tokens: introspection vs. local JWT validation, and revocation
lessons.objective: Decide how a resource server checks a token, and understand what revocation actually does.
lessons.content:
A resource server holding a bearer token has two ways to trust it, and they trade freshness against scale.

Local JWT validation — a self-contained JWT is verified against the issuer's signing keys (JWKS) with no network call. Fast and stateless, but the token stays valid until its exp: you cannot un-issue it early.

Introspection (RFC 7662) — for opaque reference tokens the API POSTs the token to /introspect with its own client credentials and reads back active (true/false) plus metadata like scope, aud, exp, and a cnf claim for sender-constrained tokens. Introspection reflects revocation immediately, at the cost of a round trip — cache positive results only up to exp. The endpoint MUST authenticate its caller and return exactly {"active":false} for an inactive token, or it becomes a token oracle.

Revocation (RFC 7009) is the write side of the same lifecycle. A client POSTs to /revoke; the AS returns 200 even for an unknown token, deliberately, so the endpoint can't be used to probe validity. Revoking a refresh token cascades to its access tokens (and, under rotation, the whole family). Whether an API sees the effect at once depends on how it validates: introspection catches it immediately, a local JWT survives until exp. That is why revocation is paired with short access-token lifetimes.

lessons.title: Logout done right: RP-initiated, front-channel, back-channel
lessons.objective: Distinguish the three OIDC logout mechanisms and see why single logout is hard.
lessons.content:
Signing out of one app is easy; signing out of an SSO session shared by many apps is not. OIDC splits the problem into three specifications.

RP-Initiated Logout starts it. The Relying Party clears its own session, then redirects the browser to the IdP's end_session_endpoint with an id_token_hint and a pre-registered post_logout_redirect_uri. The IdP ends its own SSO session and redirects back. This ends the session at the IdP — but not at the other RPs that joined the same SSO session.

Propagating to those other RPs is a separate concern with two mechanisms. Front-Channel Logout runs through the browser: the IdP's logout page renders one hidden iframe per RP, each loading that RP's frontchannel_logout_uri to clear its cookie. It needs no server-to-server path, but it is best-effort — modern browsers partition or block third-party cookies (Safari ITP, Firefox ETP, Chrome), the IdP gets no confirmation, and CSP or X-Frame-Options can silently kill a frame, so expect partial logout. Back-Channel Logout is the reliable path: the IdP POSTs a signed logout token (a JWT with an events claim plus sub and/or sid) directly to each RP's backchannel_logout_uri, no browser involved. The RP validates it like an ID token — signature, iss, aud, events, and no nonce — then destroys the matching sessions.

Single logout is hard because every RP must cooperate, front-channel delivery is unverifiable, and clearing a session does not revoke tokens already issued: access tokens live until exp unless the RP also revokes or introspects. Keep them short-lived as a backstop.

lessons.title: Choosing sessions vs. tokens (and avoiding the deprecated Implicit flow)
lessons.objective: Pick a session representation on purpose, and recognize why Implicit was replaced.
lessons.content:
How should a system remember an authenticated user across requests? Three shapes, with the same underlying tension — revocation and freshness versus scale and statelessness, plus the browser-security profile (XSS vs. CSRF).

Server-side session cookie — an opaque ID in an HttpOnly cookie, with state in a session store. Revocation is instant (delete the session); ideal for classic first-party web apps.

Stateless JWT — a self-contained signed token verified locally, scaling without any central lookup. The cost is revocation: it needs short TTLs plus a denylist to un-issue early.

Reference token + introspection — an opaque bearer token the API introspects (or caches) at the AS, giving central revocation while keeping the token contents opaque.

Whatever you choose, do not reach for the ⛔ deprecated Implicit flow. It returned tokens directly in the redirect URL fragment, exposing them to browser history, referrer leakage, and script access, with no client authentication and no refresh-token rotation. The OAuth 2.0 Security BCP forbids response_type=token and OAuth 2.1 removes the flow entirely. Its replacement is Authorization Code + PKCE: a code exchanged over the back channel, proof-bound with PKCE, and eligible for refresh-token rotation. Migrating a legacy SPA means switching response_type from id_token token to code plus PKCE, and rotating any long-lived tokens issued under Implicit.

quiz.q: A previously rotated refresh token is presented again at the token endpoint. What should the authorization server do?
choices: Silently issue a new access token; rotation makes replay harmless
Revoke the entire token family and force interactive re-authentication
Return the same access token it issued the first time
Extend the family's sliding expiry window
quiz.explain: A rotated token should never be seen again. Its reuse means two parties hold copies and one is a thief. The AS cannot tell which, so it revokes the whole family and forces re-authentication — this is reuse detection.

quiz.q: A resource server validates a self-contained JWT locally against the JWKS. An admin revokes that token. When does the API stop honoring it?
choices: Immediately, because revocation propagates to JWKS
Not until the token's exp, unless the API also introspects or checks a denylist
After the next refresh rotation
Only when the user next signs in
quiz.explain: Local JWT validation is stateless: the token stays valid until exp regardless of revocation. To get immediate effect, validate via introspection (which reflects revocation at once) or keep access-token lifetimes short.

quiz.q: Why does the RFC 7009 revocation endpoint return 200 even for a token it has never seen?
choices: To signal the token was successfully created
So the endpoint cannot be used as an oracle to probe token validity
Because unknown tokens are always still active
To trigger a retry from the client
quiz.explain: Returning 200 for unknown or already-invalid tokens is deliberate: a differentiated response would let a caller test whether a given token is valid. The endpoint must not become a validity oracle.

quiz.q: Which logout mechanism is the reliable one for propagating a single logout to other RPs, and why?
choices: Front-channel, because iframes always render
RP-initiated, because it clears the IdP session
Back-channel, because the IdP POSTs a signed logout token server-to-server with no dependence on browser cookies
They are equally reliable
quiz.explain: Front-channel logout runs through browser iframes and is best-effort — third-party-cookie blocking and CSP cause partial logout, with no confirmation to the IdP. Back-channel logout delivers a validated logout-token JWT directly to each RP, independent of the browser, so it is the reliable path.

quiz.q: A legacy SPA uses the OIDC Implicit flow (response_type=id_token token). What is the recommended migration?
choices: Keep Implicit but add longer token lifetimes
Switch to the Resource Owner Password Credentials grant
Move to Authorization Code + PKCE and rotate any long-lived tokens issued under Implicit
Add a silent-renewal iframe to keep it compliant
quiz.explain: Implicit is deprecated: it leaks tokens in the URL fragment, has no client authentication, and cannot use refresh-token rotation. The Security BCP and OAuth 2.1 replace it with Authorization Code + PKCE — a back-channel code exchange bound with PKCE.

stages.title: Authorization Models
stages.summary: The five ways systems decide what a proven identity may do: roles, attributes, relationships, externalized policy, and the token-time vs. runtime split. How each model works, where each breaks, and a rule of thumb for picking one.

lessons.title: RBAC — roles, hierarchy, and role explosion
lessons.objective: Model access by job function and recognize when roles stop scaling.
lessons.content:
Role-Based Access Control decides access by role, not by listing permissions per user. Users are assigned one or more roles; each role bundles a set of permissions — an action on a resource type, e.g. invoice:approve. A subject may act if any assigned role grants the matching permission. This is the ANSI/INCITS 359 model: the core relations are User → Role (assignment) and Role → Permission (grant).

Role hierarchy adds senior-to-junior inheritance — a senior role automatically gets every junior role's permissions, so you define "Auditor" once and let "Senior Auditor" inherit it. Optional sessions activate only a subset of a user's roles at a time, keeping least privilege (constrained RBAC). Separation of Duty guards against fraud: the person who creates a payment cannot also approve it (enforce static SoD at assignment, dynamic SoD at activation).

RBAC is the default in enterprise apps and cloud IAM (AWS IAM roles, Kubernetes RBAC, Entra ID). It fits when access maps cleanly onto stable job functions. Its failure mode is role explosion: the moment roles start encoding data values — Approver-EU-Tier1, Approver-US-Tier2 — the role count races toward the user count and you have rebuilt ABAC badly. RBAC alone cannot express "owner of this record" or "same department as the resource"; do not fake those with roles — that is the signal to move contextual conditions into attributes or relationships.

lessons.title: ABAC — attributes and policies
lessons.objective: Express context- and data-dependent access as boolean rules over attributes.
lessons.content:
Attribute-Based Access Control decides access by evaluating attributes against policies rather than static role grants. A decision is a function of four attribute categories (NIST SP 800-162):

Subject — who is asking: department, clearance, employment type, group.
Resource — what is being acted on: classification, owner, tenant, data region.
Action — the operation: read, write, approve, delete.
Environment — the context: time of day, source IP, device posture, risk score.

A policy is a boolean rule over these, e.g. "Permit read if subject.clearance >= resource.classification AND subject.region == resource.region AND env.deviceManaged == true." Because conditions compare values at request time, ABAC expresses rules that would require an explosion of roles under RBAC — multi-tenant isolation, data-residency, clearance models, time- or location-bounded access.

The tradeoffs are real. Attribute integrity is everything: ABAC is only as trustworthy as its attribute sources, so source them from signed tokens or authoritative systems, never from a spoofable client header. Choose an explicit combining algorithm (deny-overrides, permit-overrides, first-applicable) with a safe default, and treat an Indeterminate result (attribute missing, source down) as Deny for sensitive resources. Watch attribute staleness: a cache TTL on a revoked clearance is a window of over-privilege.

lessons.title: ReBAC — relationships and Google Zanzibar
lessons.objective: Authorize from an object graph using tuples and Check.
lessons.content:
Relationship-Based Access Control decides access from the relationships between subjects and objects rather than from roles or standalone attributes. Google Zanzibar is the canonical implementation and the model behind SpiceDB, OpenFGA, Ory Keto, and Auth0 FGA. Its building blocks:

Relation tuple — the atomic fact, written object#relation@user, e.g. document:readme#owner@user:anna ("anna is an owner of document readme").
Userset — a set of users defined by a relation, so a tuple's "user" can itself be a group: document:readme#viewer@group:eng#member gives groups-as-subjects.
Namespace schema — per-type config with userset rewrites that compose relations transitively: viewer = viewer + editor (editors are viewers), viewer = viewer + parent->viewer (inherit from a parent folder).
Check(object, relation, user) — the authorization API: is this user related to this object via this relation? It returns a boolean, walking the tuple graph and the rewrites.

ReBAC shines for fine-grained, per-object access at scale: "who can view this specific document," nested folders, org/team hierarchies, Google-Docs-style sharing — object graphs that RBAC role explosion and ABAC attribute plumbing cannot express cleanly. Two cautions dominate. A zookie (consistency token) binds a Check to a minimum snapshot; pass the zookie from a permission-revoking write into later Checks to avoid the "new enemy" problem — a stale replica leaking content after a revoke. And writes must be authorized: anyone who can write document:x#owner@user:self has just granted themselves access, so guard the write path.

lessons.title: PBAC — external policy engines and PEP/PDP/PIP/PAP
lessons.objective: Externalize decisions into a policy engine and name the four cooperating roles.
lessons.content:
Policy-Based Access Control externalizes the authorization decision into a dedicated policy engine the application calls instead of hard-coding if checks. The engine evaluates declarative policy against an input document (subject, action, resource, context) and returns a decision. Two dominant implementations: Open Policy Agent (OPA), a general-purpose engine whose policies are written in Rego and distributed as signed bundles; and AWS Cedar, a purpose-built language of permit/forbid statements over principal, action, resource, and context that is analyzable and forbid-overrides by design.

Both realize the reference architecture that XACML named and that is now shared vocabulary:

PEP — Policy Enforcement Point. Sits in the request path (API gateway or sidecar), builds the decision request, calls the PDP, and enforces the result. It holds no policy logic.
PDP — Policy Decision Point. Evaluates policy and returns a decision, optionally with obligations (things the PEP must do, e.g. redact a field) and advice.
PIP — Policy Information Point. Supplies attributes the request lacks (department, owner, risk score) from directories or services.
PAP — Policy Administration Point. Where policy is authored, versioned, and distributed — not in the request path.

The payoff is separation of decision from enforcement: policy changes at the PAP reach the PDPs without redeploying services, and PBAC can express RBAC, ABAC, or relationship rules — it is a mechanism, not a distinct model. The rules: fail closed (an unreachable or erroring PDP must deny, never allow), sign and verify bundles so a compromised control plane cannot ship an allow-everything policy, and treat decision logs as both audit evidence and sensitive data.

lessons.title: Scopes vs. claims vs. entitlements
lessons.objective: Separate coarse token-time authority from fine-grained runtime decisions.
lessons.content:
Three primitives operate at different layers and are constantly confused:

OAuth scopes are a token-time, coarse grant. A scope like invoices.read names a capability the client asked for and the user consented to; it bounds what the client may attempt on the user's behalf — a ceiling on delegated authority, fixed for the life of the token, not per-object permission.

Claims are assertions about the subject or authorization context carried in the token: identity claims (sub, email) in the ID token, authorization claims (roles, groups, tenant, acr) in the access token. They are what the issuer stated at issuance — readable without a network call, but only as fresh as the token.

Entitlements are fine-grained, runtime authorization facts — "may user U perform action A on this specific resource R" — resolved at the resource against live policy and data. They are not a token format; they are the decision an authorization model (RBAC, ReBAC, ABAC) produces per request.

The relationship is a funnel: scope gates whether the client may even ask; claims carry who the subject is and coarse context; entitlement decides this exact operation on this exact object, now. A request must pass all three. The cardinal rule: scope is a ceiling, not a permission — invoices.write means "the client may attempt writes," never "the user may write this invoice." Enforcing only scope is the classic broken-object-level-authorization (BOLA/IDOR) flaw, so always add the instance-level entitlement check at the resource, and do not trust role/group claims past their freshness — re-decide sensitive actions against live data.

quiz.q: A team keeps adding roles like Approver-EU-Tier1 and Approver-US-Tier2 as new regions and tiers appear. What is happening and what does it signal?
choices: Healthy use of role hierarchy; nothing to change
Role explosion — the distinctions belong in attributes or relationships, not new roles
Separation of Duty being enforced correctly
A sign to remove the role hierarchy entirely
quiz.explain: When roles start encoding data values (region, tier, tenant, ownership), the role count races toward the user count. That is role explosion, and the contextual conditions belong in ABAC attributes or ReBAC relationships instead of ever more roles.

quiz.q: A policy reads: Permit if subject.clearance >= resource.classification AND env.deviceManaged == true. Which authorization model is this?
choices: RBAC, because clearance is a role
ReBAC, because it relates a subject to a resource
ABAC, because the decision is a boolean rule over subject, resource, and environment attributes
PBAC, because it is written as a policy
quiz.explain: The decision compares attribute values (subject clearance, resource classification, environment device posture) at request time. That is ABAC. A policy engine could evaluate it, but the model — the shape of the decision — is attribute-based.

quiz.q: In Google Zanzibar, after revoking someone's access you want your next Check to reflect the revoke rather than read a stale replica. What do you use?
choices: A userset rewrite
The Expand API
A permit-overrides combining algorithm
The zookie (consistency token) from the revoking write
quiz.explain: A zookie encodes a snapshot timestamp. Passing the zookie from a permission-revoking write into later Checks forces an at-least-as-fresh read, closing the 'new enemy' window where a stale ACL could still permit access.

quiz.q: In the PEP/PDP/PIP/PAP pattern, which component fetches attributes the decision request is missing, such as a user's department or a resource owner?
choices: PEP (Policy Enforcement Point)
PDP (Policy Decision Point)
PIP (Policy Information Point)
PAP (Policy Administration Point)
quiz.explain: The PIP supplies attributes the request lacks, pulled from directories, databases, or risk services. The PEP enforces, the PDP decides, and the PAP authors and distributes policy out of the request path.

quiz.q: A token carries the scope invoices.write. A request tries to edit invoice #42 that the subject does not own. What is the correct outcome?
choices: Allow — the scope grants write access to invoices
Deny — scope is a ceiling on what the client may attempt; the resource must still check the instance-level entitlement
Allow — scopes always imply per-object permission
Deny — invoices.write is an identity claim, not a scope
quiz.explain: Scope bounds what the client may attempt, never per-object permission. Enforcing only scope is the classic BOLA/IDOR flaw; the resource must resolve the runtime entitlement (does this subject own or relate to invoice #42?) before allowing the write.

stages.title: Identity Lifecycle & Directories
stages.summary: How identities are born, changed, and killed off — HR-driven joiner/mover/leaver orchestration, SCIM provisioning, access recertification, factor enrollment, and the directories that back it all — with the leaver case as the highest-risk moment of the whole lifecycle.

lessons.title: Joiner, Mover, Leaver orchestration
lessons.objective: See identity as event-driven state that HR authorizes and IGA enforces — and why the leaver is the riskiest event.
lessons.content:
An identity has a lifecycle, and it is event-driven and attribute-based. The pattern is always the same three moving parts:

HR is the source of truth for who exists and what they are — it emits the joiner, mover, and leaver events. The IGA engine is authoritative for what access that implies — it re-evaluates policy on every event. The IdP and downstream apps are the targets that get provisioned or deprovisioned.

Joiner — create the identity, grant birthright access (the baseline every employee in that role/department/location gets automatically, no ticket required), provision apps, issue credentials, prompt for MFA enrollment.

Mover — an attribute changes (new department, new title). IGA re-evaluates: add the new entitlements and revoke the stale ones. The stale-revoke half is the one organizations forget, and it is exactly how privilege creep accumulates.

Leaver — the highest-risk transition. A departing person still holding live access is an active attacker surface. Timely deprovisioning means: disable the account, kill running sessions and refresh tokens (disabling the account does not evict a session already minted), revoke app access, reclaim licenses, then archive and delete after the retention window. Speed matters — the gap between the last day and the disable is pure exposure.

Two edge cases every design must handle: out-of-order events (a leaver arriving before a pending mover finishes — IGA reconciles to the latest authoritative state) and a reconciliation sweep that compares intended state against actual state to catch orphaned accounts the events missed.

lessons.title: SCIM provisioning
lessons.objective: Understand the standard protocol that turns 'IGA provisions an app' into concrete REST calls.
lessons.content:
When IGA or the IdP "provisions an app," it is almost always speaking SCIM (System for Cross-domain Identity Management) 2.0 — RFC 7643 for the schema, RFC 7644 for the protocol. SCIM is the standard REST/JSON wire format for pushing users and groups from a client (the IdP/IGA, the provisioning source) into a service provider (the downstream app exposing /Users and /Groups endpoints).

The user CRUD lifecycle maps to plain HTTP verbs:

  • POST /Users — create a new user, returns 201 with a server-assigned id (this is the joiner)
  • PATCH /Users/{id} — partial update (add/replace/remove ops)
  • PUT /Users/{id} — full replacement of the resource
  • PATCH /Groups/{id} — add or remove a single member without rewriting the whole group (this is the mover)
  • DELETE /Users/{id} — often mapped to soft-delete rather than a hard purge

The details that separate a toy client from a production one are the error and edge cases: a 409 Conflict on create (the userName already exists — the client GETs and switches to PATCH/PUT), soft-delete via active=false (deactivate but preserve the record, the norm for a leaver under retention), and 429 Too Many Requests rate limiting with a Retry-After back-off. Okta, Entra ID, OneLogin, and SailPoint all speak SCIM to their app connectors.

lessons.title: Access reviews and certification
lessons.objective: Learn the detective control that catches the privilege creep the event-driven flows let through.
lessons.content:
Joiner and mover are preventive — they try to keep access correct at the moment of change. But access still drifts: privileges granted by exception and never removed, entitlements a forgotten mover left behind, orphaned grants. Access review (recertification) is the periodic detective control that asks: does everyone who has access still deserve it?

The IGA engine generates a campaign — a scoped, time-bounded batch of review items, each pairing a user (or role/entitlement) with a reviewer, usually the line manager or the resource owner. For every item the reviewer must certify (affirm it is still needed) or revoke (mark it for removal). Revocations flow into remediation, which deprovisions the access through the very same machinery as leaver offboarding.

Two design defaults matter. Auto-revoke on no response: items left undecided at the deadline default to revoke — a secure default, not silent retention. And beware rubber-stamping: bulk-approving a whole campaign in one click technically closes the items but hollows out the control.

Auditors care because certifications produce evidence — a signed, timestamped record that a responsible human affirmatively decided each grant is still appropriate. SOX and ISO 27001 effectively mandate them, and high-risk or privileged access is reviewed on a tighter cadence than baseline access.

lessons.title: Enrollment: MFA and FIDO2 passkeys
lessons.objective: Contrast registering a shared-secret factor with registering a phishing-resistant key pair.
lessons.content:
A joiner has an account, but not yet a strong factor. Enrollment is the act of registering one — and it always happens inside an authenticated (often freshly re-authenticated) session, because adding a factor is itself a sensitive operation.

MFA enrollment (TOTP). The server generates a per-user secret and hands it over as a QR code (an otpauth:// URI) plus a manual key; the authenticator app derives 6-digit time-based codes (RFC 6238). The user proves possession by typing the first generated code before the factor is activated, and the server issues one-time backup codes. Rules that keep it safe: the server generates and owns the secret (never accept a client-supplied one), treat the factor as inactive until proof-of-possession succeeds, verify against the current time window with small skew tolerance, and rate-limit attempts. SMS/voice OTP follows the same shape but is a weaker, phishable channel.

FIDO2 / passkey registration. A different and stronger model. In the WebAuthn attestation ceremony the Relying Party issues a challenge and creation options; the browser calls navigator.credentials.create(); the authenticator generates a public/private key pair scoped to the RP ID, keeps the private key, and returns an attestation object. The server validates it and stores only the credential public key + credential ID. Because there is no shared secret to phish and the key is bound to the origin, passkeys are phishing-resistant where TOTP is not. Server-side checks: the clientDataJSON.type is webauthn.create, the challenge matches and is single-use, the origin is expected, and excludeCredentials stops an already-enrolled authenticator from double-registering.

lessons.title: Directories: AD logon and hybrid sync
lessons.objective: Know how domain logon works and how the three hybrid sign-in models differ.
lessons.content:
Under all of this sits a directory — historically Active Directory. Interactive logon is what happens when a user signs in to a domain-joined Windows machine. The logon stack (Winlogon, LSASS and its Security Support Providers) turns credentials into domain authentication via Negotiate (SPNEGO): Windows prefers Kerberos — which yields a cached TGT and later service tickets — and only falls back to NTLM when Kerberos is unavailable (no reachable KDC, access by IP literal, a local account, or a target with no Service Principal Name). The user's group SIDs ride in the Kerberos PAC, from which Windows builds the logon token. NTLM is Legacy and discouraged: it is exposed to relay attacks, pass-the-hash, and offline cracking, so restrict it and prefer Kerberos.

When the directory extends to the cloud, there are three hybrid sign-in models — the tradeoff is where the password is actually validated:

  • Password hash sync (PHS) — a sync agent copies a hash of the on-prem NT hash (re-hashed with PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256, salted) up to the cloud IdP. Sign-in is validated entirely in the cloud, so it keeps working during an on-prem outage and needs no inbound firewall openings. The plaintext never leaves the domain controller, and the stored value cannot be replayed on-prem. It also enables leaked-credential detection.
  • Pass-through authentication (PTA) — same password, but validated live against on-prem AD at each sign-in via a lightweight agent. No password hash is stored in the cloud, but sign-in now depends on on-prem availability.
  • Federation — the cloud redirects authentication to an on-prem STS (e.g. ADFS); the on-prem system fully owns the credential check and returns a token. Most control, most infrastructure, and the cloud never sees a verifier at all.

Remember the leaver angle here too: a disabled AD account must sync as disabled so cloud sign-in is blocked — verify sync scoping so deprovisioning actually propagates.

quiz.q: An employee is terminated at 5pm. IT disables the AD account at 5:05pm but the person keeps accessing a SaaS app for another hour. What was most likely missed?
choices: Birthright access was never granted
Running sessions and refresh tokens were not revoked
The joiner event never fired
SCIM returned a 409 Conflict
quiz.explain: Disabling the account stops new logons but does not evict a session or refresh token already minted. Timely leaver deprovisioning must kill live sessions and tokens, not just disable the account — the leaver is the highest-risk transition precisely because of gaps like this.

quiz.q: An IGA engine needs to add a single user to one group in a downstream app without rewriting the group's entire membership. Which SCIM call fits?
choices: PUT /Users/{id}
POST /Users
PATCH /Groups/{id}
DELETE /Groups/{id}
quiz.explain: A PATCH to /Groups/{id} carries a targeted add/remove Operations patch, changing one member without replacing the whole members array. POST /Users creates a user; PUT fully replaces a resource.

quiz.q: Why is a periodic access certification campaign considered a detective control rather than a preventive one?
choices: It blocks access at the moment an attribute changes
It runs before the joiner is provisioned
It catches privilege creep and stale grants that the event-driven joiner/mover flows already let through
It only applies to service accounts
quiz.explain: Joiner and mover are preventive — they fix access at the moment of change. Certification is detective: it periodically re-checks existing access to catch drift, exception grants never removed, and orphaned entitlements the events missed.

quiz.q: What makes FIDO2 passkey registration phishing-resistant in a way that TOTP enrollment is not?
choices: TOTP codes are longer than passkey signatures
The passkey uses an origin-bound public/private key pair with no shared secret to steal, while TOTP relies on a shared secret and a code the user can be tricked into typing
Passkeys are sent over SMS
The server supplies the passkey secret to the client
quiz.explain: In WebAuthn the authenticator generates a key pair scoped to the RP ID and keeps the private key; the server stores only the public key, and the ceremony is bound to the origin. There is no shared secret to phish and a code cannot be replayed on a lookalike site — unlike a TOTP code the user types.

quiz.q: An organization wants cloud sign-in to keep working even during a complete on-prem Active Directory outage, with no inbound firewall openings. Which hybrid model fits best?
choices: Federation to an on-prem STS
Pass-through authentication (PTA)
Password hash synchronization (PHS)
NTLM fallback
quiz.explain: PHS validates the password entirely in the cloud from a synced (re-hashed, salted) verifier, so sign-in survives an on-prem outage and needs no inbound openings. PTA and federation both depend on on-prem availability at sign-in time.

stages.title: Strong & Phishing-Resistant Authentication
stages.summary: What makes an authentication factor phishing-resistant, and what makes one weak: public-key passkeys vs. shared-secret OTP, how Kerberos tickets prove identity without resending a password, how to choose an MFA factor, and how adaptive and step-up policies gate access on risk.

lessons.title: WebAuthn & passkeys: why public-key auth resists phishing
lessons.objective: Understand why a passkey cannot be handed to a look-alike site the way a password or OTP can.
lessons.content:
A password is a shared secret: the user knows it and the server stores a copy. Anything the user can type, the user can be tricked into typing somewhere else — including a phishing page that relays it onward. One-time codes have the same flaw: a code the user reads and retypes can be relayed in real time.

WebAuthn / passkeys break that pattern. Registration stores a public key on the server; the matching private key never leaves the authenticator (Touch ID, Windows Hello, a phone, or a security key). To log in, the server sends a random challenge; the authenticator signs it after a local user verification gesture (biometric or PIN), and the server checks the signature against the stored public key. There is no shared secret to steal and no bearer token to replay — the proof is a fresh digital signature.

The phishing resistance comes from origin binding, enforced by the browser, not the user. Credentials are scoped to the site's RP ID, and the browser stamps the real origin into the signed clientDataJSON. A look-alike domain has a different RP ID, so the authenticator simply has no credential to offer and the server rejects any assertion whose origin does not match. The user cannot be socially engineered into defeating this, because there is nothing to type or read aloud.

The server still must verify everything: the signature, that the challenge matches the single-use one it issued, that the origin and rpIdHash are expected, and that the user-presence and (when required) user-verification flags are set. A signature counter that goes backwards can signal a cloned authenticator.
