lessons.title: Kerberos: tickets and the AS / TGS / AP exchanges
lessons.objective: See how Kerberos proves identity to many services without re-sending the password each time.
lessons.content:
Kerberos is the ticket-based protocol behind Windows domain logon and kinit on Linux/macOS. Its goal is single sign-on: prove who you are once, then reach many services without re-entering credentials. A trusted Key Distribution Center (KDC) issues encrypted tickets that vouch for the user, and three exchanges chain together:

AS exchange (AS-REQ / AS-REP) — the initial authentication. The client proves knowledge of the user's long-term key (derived from the password) via encrypted pre-auth data and receives a Ticket-Granting Ticket (TGT), encrypted with the KDC's own krbtgt key so it is opaque to the client, plus a TGT session key. The password is never sent again after this.

TGS exchange (TGS-REQ / TGS-REP) — the client presents the TGT to ask for a service ticket for one specific service, named by its Service Principal Name (e.g. HTTP/web01.example.com). The KDC returns a ticket encrypted with that service's account key. This is transparent — no password prompt.

AP exchange (AP-REQ / AP-REP) — the client presents the service ticket to the service itself along with a fresh authenticator (a timestamp encrypted with the session key). The service decrypts the ticket with its own key and checks the authenticator against a replay cache. If mutual authentication is requested, the service returns an AP-REP proving it too holds the key. The KDC is not contacted for this step.

Because each ticket is encrypted for a specific key holder and each authenticator is fresh and single-use, a captured message cannot be replayed against a different service — the identity proof travels as tickets, not as a reusable password.

lessons.title: Choosing an MFA factor: strong vs. weak
lessons.objective: Rank the common second factors by phishing resistance and know why SMS is the weakest.
lessons.content:
Not all multi-factor options are equal. The overriding principle is phishing resistance: can a real-time proxy sitting between the user and the site steal or relay the factor? The tiers:

Phishing-resistant (preferred). FIDO2 / passkeys (WebAuthn), Windows Hello for Business, and PIV / smartcard certificates cryptographically bind the credential to the origin. There is no code to read and no secret to type, so an attacker-in-the-middle page cannot capture anything reusable. These are the recommended defaults.

Acceptable second tier. Authenticator push with number matching and TOTP (authenticator-app codes) are far better than nothing. But both are still phishable: a proxy can relay a TOTP code within its short window, and push without number matching invites MFA-fatigue approvals. Number matching hardens push; it does not make it origin-bound.

⛔ SMS and voice OTP — not a primary factor. A texted code is a shared secret the user reads and retypes, so it is trivially relayed by a phishing proxy. Worse, the delivery channel itself is attackable: SIM-swap, SS7 interception, and carrier social engineering can divert the code without ever touching the user's phone. SMS is deprecated as a primary factor; keep it only as a last-resort recovery path when nothing else is possible.

The short version: a passkey is strong because the secret never leaves the device and the browser enforces origin binding; an SMS OTP is weak because the secret is disclosed to the user, is replayable, and rides an insecure channel.

lessons.title: Adaptive & step-up authentication: gating on risk
lessons.objective: Understand how risk signals and sensitive-action triggers decide between allow, step-up, and deny.
lessons.content:
A fixed "always MFA" or "never MFA" policy is too blunt. Two related patterns make authentication context-dependent.

Risk-based adaptive authentication acts at sign-in. The IdP gathers signals — device posture and fingerprint, geolocation, login velocity, IP / ASN reputation, threat intelligence, leaked-credential hits — and a risk engine scores them into a level. A policy maps the level to one of three outcomes: Allow (primary factor is enough, issue tokens), Step-up (challenge for a stronger or additional factor, then re-evaluate), or Deny (a hard signal like impossible travel or a known-bad IP blocks and alerts). Low-risk, familiar sign-ins stay frictionless while risky ones are challenged or stopped.

Step-up authentication acts mid-session. An already-authenticated user attempts a sensitive action — a wire transfer, changing MFA methods, an admin operation — and the resource decides the session's assurance is too low. Using standard signalling (in OIDC, acr_values and max_age; RFC 9470 lets an API return an insufficient_user_authentication challenge), the IdP re-challenges for a stronger or more recent factor and re-issues a token carrying the elevated acr. The two compose: a risk engine can itself demand step-up.

Two rules make this safe. Fail closed: if a signal source is unreachable, default toward step-up or deny, never silently toward allow. Step up to phishing-resistant factors: stepping up to SMS or plain push can be relayed by an attacker-in-the-middle, defeating the point — prefer FIDO2 / passkeys for the elevated challenge. And the relying party must trust the freshly issued token's acr and auth_time, not merely its own memory that it once prompted.

quiz.q: Why can a passkey not be captured by a look-alike phishing site the way a password can?
choices: The passkey is a longer, more complex password that is harder to guess
The private key never leaves the authenticator and the browser scopes the credential to the site's RP ID and signs the real origin
Passkeys are encrypted in transit while passwords are sent in cleartext
The server emails the user a confirmation before accepting the passkey
quiz.explain: Phishing resistance comes from origin binding enforced by the browser: credentials are scoped to the RP ID and the real origin is stamped into the signed clientDataJSON. A look-alike domain has a different RP ID, so the authenticator has no credential to offer and there is no shared secret to relay.

quiz.q: In Kerberos, which exchange produces the Ticket-Granting Ticket (TGT) that lets the client obtain service tickets without re-entering the password?
choices: The AP exchange (AP-REQ / AP-REP)
The TGS exchange (TGS-REQ / TGS-REP)
The AS exchange (AS-REQ / AS-REP)
The replay-cache check
quiz.explain: The AS exchange is the initial authentication: the client proves knowledge of the user's long-term key and receives the TGT (encrypted with the krbtgt key) plus a TGT session key. The TGT is then spent in the TGS exchange to get per-service tickets.

quiz.q: Which set of MFA factors is phishing-resistant (origin-bound and not relayable by a real-time proxy)?
choices: SMS OTP, voice OTP, and email codes
FIDO2 / passkeys, Windows Hello for Business, and PIV / smartcard
TOTP authenticator codes and push without number matching
Any factor, as long as it is a second factor on top of a password
quiz.explain: FIDO2/passkeys, WHfB, and PIV/smartcard cryptographically bind the credential to the origin, so an attacker-in-the-middle cannot capture anything reusable. TOTP and push are phishable second tiers; SMS/voice codes are the weakest.

quiz.q: Why is an SMS one-time code considered a weak primary factor?
choices: Phones cannot receive text messages reliably enough
It is a shared secret the user reads and retypes, so a phishing proxy can relay it, and the delivery channel is attackable via SIM-swap and SS7
SMS codes expire too slowly to be useful
It requires a biometric that many users cannot provide
quiz.explain: A texted code is disclosed to the user and retyped, making it trivially relayable in real time, and the channel itself is vulnerable to SIM-swap, SS7 interception, and carrier social engineering. That is why SMS is deprecated as a primary factor and kept only as a last-resort recovery path.

quiz.q: A risk engine scores a sign-in as high risk because of impossible travel plus a leaked-credential hit. Under a well-designed adaptive policy, what should happen, and what is the correct default if a signal source is unreachable?
choices: Allow the sign-in; default to allow when signals are missing
Deny and alert on the hard signals; fail closed (default to step-up or deny) when a signal source is unreachable
Silently downgrade to a password-only prompt in both cases
Always deny every sign-in regardless of score
quiz.explain: Hard signals like impossible travel and leaked-credential matches should trigger the Deny outcome with an alert. And an unreachable risk engine or feed must fail closed toward step-up or deny, never silently toward allow, so missing signals cannot become a free pass.

stages.title: Cloud IAM & Workload Identity
stages.summary: How machines get cloud access without stored secrets: temporary credentials from STS, OIDC federation for keyless CI, policy gates at token issuance, and workload-bound identities from Kubernetes to SPIFFE. One theme runs through all of it — replace long-lived stored keys with short-lived, federated, workload-bound credentials.

lessons.title: AWS STS AssumeRole: temporary credentials and role trust
lessons.objective: Understand how an already-authenticated principal trades into a role for short-lived credentials, and why two policies must agree.
lessons.content:
AWS Security Token Service (STS) issues temporary security credentials — an AccessKeyId, a SecretAccessKey, and a SessionToken — that expire. The core API is sts:AssumeRole: an already-authenticated principal (an IAM user, another role, or a service) assumes a task-specific IAM role and receives credentials scoped to that role's permissions.

Whether the assume succeeds is decided by two policies that must both allow it:

  • the caller's identity policy — it must permit Action: sts:AssumeRole on the target role's ARN; and
  • the role's trust policy (the AssumeRolePolicyDocument) — it names which principals are allowed to assume the role.

A broad trust policy is the classic misconfiguration, so scope the Principal and add conditions like aws:PrincipalOrgID or aws:SourceAccount. For third-party/vendor access, require an ExternalId to defeat the confused-deputy problem — and never let the vendor choose it or reuse it across customers.

Credentials are valid for DurationSeconds (15 minutes up to the role's MaxSessionDuration, capped at 12 hours; role chaining caps at 1 hour). You can narrow them further with an inline session policy — effective permissions are the intersection of the role's policies and the session policy, so a session policy can only restrict, never grant beyond the role. This is the foundation: short-lived, auditable credentials in place of long-lived IAM user access keys that sit in a config file waiting to leak.

lessons.title: Keyless CI via OIDC: AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity
lessons.objective: See how a signed OIDC token replaces stored AWS keys entirely, and why the trust policy must pin both aud and sub.
lessons.content:
sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity exchanges a signed OIDC ID token (a JWT) from an external identity provider for temporary AWS credentials — with no long-lived AWS access keys involved at all. The call is unsigned, because the JWT itself is the proof.

The flagship use is GitHub Actions deploying to AWS keylessly. The workflow asks GitHub for an OIDC token from token.actions.githubusercontent.com, calls AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity, and receives short-lived credentials scoped to the deploy role. The stored AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID secret disappears completely.

Setup requires an IAM OIDC identity provider that records the issuer URL and a certificate thumbprint (AWS now validates most issuers directly against the issuer's published JWKS). STS then validates the JWT signature, that iss matches the provider, that aud is in the allowed ClientIDList, that exp has not passed, and finally the trust-policy claim conditions.

Those conditions are where security lives. The trust policy keys are prefixed by the issuer host, e.g. token.actions.githubusercontent.com:aud and :sub. Always pin both: use StringEquals on aud, and a tightly scoped StringLike on sub such as repo:my-org/my-repo:ref:refs/heads/main. An aud-only policy on the GitHub issuer trusts every repository on GitHub; a wildcard sub like repo:my-org/* lets the wrong branch or a fork assume the role. This is the same mechanism EKS uses for IRSA — projected ServiceAccount tokens exchanged for role credentials.

lessons.title: Entra Conditional Access at token issuance
lessons.objective: Understand how a policy engine evaluates request signals at the moment a token is minted, and how that fits Zero Trust.
lessons.content:
Not every gate is about swapping keys — sometimes the question is whether a token should be issued at all, given the context of the request. Conditional Access (CA) is Microsoft Entra ID's policy engine, and it runs at the moment a token is about to be issued.

The Entra authorization endpoint evaluates every enabled CA policy against the signals of the request: the user or group, the target cloud app, the client app type, sign-in and user risk (from Identity Protection), device state (compliant / Entra-joined), network location (named locations, trusted IPs), and authentication context.

Each matching policy produces two kinds of output:

  • Grant controls — block, require MFA, require a compliant device, require an approved client app, require terms of use, require password change.
  • Session controls — sign-in frequency, persistent browser, app-enforced restrictions, and Continuous Access Evaluation.

The union of all matching policies must be satisfied before a token is minted. This is Zero Trust's "verify explicitly" in practice. A few operational truths: CA is fail-closed for block policies but only evaluates signals it actually has — so disable legacy authentication, or password-only protocols will bypass your MFA policies. Always keep a break-glass account excluded from CA to avoid tenant lock-out, and validate new policies in report-only mode with the What-If tool first. Location signals rely on source IP and can be spoofed; prefer device compliance and phishing-resistant MFA over IP allow-lists. Pair CA with Continuous Access Evaluation so revocation is near-real-time rather than waiting for token expiry.

lessons.title: GCP Workload Identity Federation
lessons.objective: Follow the token-exchange-then-impersonate pattern that lets external workloads reach Google Cloud without a downloadable key.
lessons.content:
Google Cloud's answer to the stored-key problem for workloads running outside GCP — GitHub Actions, AWS, Azure, on-prem OIDC/SAML IdPs — is Workload Identity Federation. It is the recommended replacement for downloading a service account JSON key.

The external workload presents a credential its own IdP already issues: an OIDC ID token, an AWS GetCallerIdentity signature, or a SAML assertion. Google's Security Token Service (sts.googleapis.com) exchanges that for a short-lived federated access token. The workload then usually impersonates a service account via generateAccessToken to obtain the final Google credential — a two-leg pattern: exchange, then impersonate.

Trust is defined by a Workload Identity Pool containing one or more Providers. Each provider pins the external issuer and the allowed audience, and carries an attribute mapping written in CEL — for example google.subject = assertion.sub and attribute.repository = assertion.repository. The federated identity is expressed as a principalSet:// member such as one keyed on attribute.repository/ORG/REPO, and SA impersonation is granted to that member.

The critical control is the provider's attribute_condition (also CEL): set it so only the intended repo, branch, or AWS account can federate. A missing condition trusts every token the issuer can mint. Always validate the audience so tokens minted for one provider cannot be replayed to another, and enforce iam.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation so teams cannot quietly fall back to keys. Same principle as AWS web-identity, expressed in Google's vocabulary.

lessons.title: Non-human identity: SPIFFE/SPIRE and projected ServiceAccount tokens
lessons.objective: Understand attestation-based, platform-neutral workload identity and the audience-bound Kubernetes token that feeds cloud exchanges.
lessons.content:
Federation still needs the workload to already have a token to present. Where does that first identity come from? Two answers close the loop, both replacing on-disk secrets with attested, short-lived, workload-bound credentials.

Kubernetes projected ServiceAccount tokens. A projected token is a short-lived, audience-bound OIDC JWT that the kubelet obtains from the API server's TokenRequest API and mounts into a Pod as a projected volume. Unlike the old, never-expiring Secret-based tokens, it has an explicit aud, a bounded exp the kubelet refreshes before it lapses, and it is bound to the Pod's lifetime. Because the cluster publishes an OIDC discovery document and JWKS, any external relying party that trusts the cluster issuer — AWS STS AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity, GCP/Azure federation, Vault — can verify it and return its own credential. The sub is system:serviceaccount:<ns>:<sa>; always map the exact subject, never namespace alone on a shared cluster. Treat legacy Secret-mounted tokens as deprecated: they never expire and are not audience-bound.

SPIFFE/SPIRE. SPIFFE defines a platform-neutral identity — the SPIFFE ID, a URI like spiffe://example.org/ns/prod/sa/frontend — carried in an SVID. SPIRE is the reference implementation: a SPIRE Server is the trust-domain signing authority and registry; a SPIRE Agent on each node performs node attestation (AWS Instance Identity Document, GCP instance identity, Kubernetes PSAT, TPM, join token) and then workload attestation (kernel peer credentials plus unix/docker/k8s selectors) before handing each workload an SVID over the Workload API. SVIDs come as an X.509-SVID (SPIFFE ID in the URI SAN, for mTLS) or a JWT-SVID (sub is the SPIFFE ID, aud names the target service). Attestation is the root of trust, TTLs are short (default 1h) with automatic rotation, and no private key is ever persisted. Together these give workloads an identity with no stored secret at all — the endpoint of the whole theme.

quiz.q: A caller has an identity policy allowing sts:AssumeRole on a role's ARN, but the assume still fails. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The credentials returned were not signed with SigV4
The role's trust policy does not name the caller as an allowed principal
The DurationSeconds was set below 15 minutes
STS only issues credentials to IAM users, not roles
quiz.explain: Two policies must both allow the assume: the caller's identity policy AND the role's trust policy (the AssumeRolePolicyDocument). If the trust policy does not name the caller as an allowed principal, the assume is denied even when the identity policy permits it.

quiz.q: A GitHub Actions role trust policy pins token.actions.githubusercontent.com:aud but has no sub condition. What is the risk?
choices: Nothing — pinning aud alone fully scopes the role to your workflow
Any repository on GitHub can mint a token that satisfies the policy and assume the role
The role can no longer be assumed by any workflow
GitHub will refuse to issue the OIDC token without a sub claim
quiz.explain: An aud-only condition on the GitHub issuer trusts every repository on GitHub, since aud identifies the audience but not which repo/branch requested the token. You must also pin a tightly scoped sub (e.g. repo:my-org/my-repo:ref:refs/heads/main) so only the intended workflow can assume the role.

quiz.q: In Entra Conditional Access, when are policies evaluated and what determines the outcome?
choices: After a token is issued, and only network location matters
At the moment a token is about to be issued, and the union of all matching policies must be satisfied
Only during password reset, based solely on user risk
Once per day as a batch job that revokes tokens
quiz.explain: CA runs at token issuance. The authorization endpoint evaluates every enabled policy against the request's signals (user, app, risk, device, location) and the union of all matching policies' grant controls must be satisfied before a token is minted.

quiz.q: In GCP Workload Identity Federation, what happens after sts.googleapis.com returns a federated access token, and what is the key restriction on which external tokens are accepted?
choices: The workload downloads a service account key; the pool's audience is ignored
The workload usually impersonates a service account via generateAccessToken; the provider's attribute_condition restricts which tokens federate
Google immediately revokes the token; only SAML assertions are accepted
The federated token is permanent; only the sub claim is checked
quiz.explain: It is a two-leg pattern: the STS exchange yields a short-lived federated token, then the workload typically impersonates a service account via generateAccessToken for the final credential. A provider's attribute_condition (CEL) restricts which external tokens are accepted — a missing condition trusts every token the issuer can mint.

quiz.q: How does a Kubernetes projected ServiceAccount token differ from a legacy Secret-based ServiceAccount token?
choices: The projected token never expires and is not audience-bound
The projected token is audience-bound, has a bounded expiry the kubelet refreshes, and is tied to the Pod's lifetime
The projected token can only be used inside the cluster and never verified externally
There is no difference; both are stored as long-lived Secrets
quiz.explain: A projected token has an explicit audience (aud), a bounded expiry (exp) the kubelet refreshes before it lapses, and is bound to the Pod's lifetime. Legacy Secret-based tokens never expire and are not audience-bound, so they are treated as deprecated. Because the cluster publishes OIDC discovery + JWKS, external relying parties can still verify the projected token.

stages.title: Privileged & Adaptive Access
stages.summary: Two halves of the same discipline: minimize standing privilege so a compromised account is usually not privileged, and re-check the session continuously instead of trusting the login forever.

lessons.title: Just-in-time privilege elevation
lessons.objective: Trace the eligible → request → approve → time-bound → auto-revoke lifecycle and see why standing privilege is the thing to remove.
lessons.content:
The old model gives an administrator a privileged role permanently. The problem is standing privilege: if that account is phished, it is privileged the moment it is compromised. Just-in-time (JIT) elevation flips the default — the identity is only made eligible for the role, and the privilege sits dormant until it is activated.

The lifecycle is a chain of gates:

Eligible — a standing assignment that grants nothing on its own. Eligibility is not access.
Request / activate — the admin supplies a justification (often bound to a change ticket) and passes a fresh, phishing-resistant MFA challenge — a valid session is not enough, because activation is the moment privilege is actually conferred.
Approve — sensitive roles pause for a human approver; lower-tier roles may auto-approve after MFA + justification.
Time-bound — activation grants the role for a short, scoped window: the least role, for the least time, on the least scope.
Auto-revoke — when the window expires the assignment is removed automatically, with no user action, and the identity returns to zero standing privilege.

The payoff: a compromised admin account is usually not currently privileged, which shrinks the attack window to the rare, logged, justified moments of activation. Microsoft Entra PIM is the canonical implementation; AWS temporary role assumption and third-party PAM follow the same pattern.

lessons.title: Break-glass emergency access
lessons.objective: Understand the sealed, monitored, rehearsed exception you keep for when the normal paths themselves fail.
lessons.content:
JIT and approval flows depend on the identity provider being up. What happens when the IdP is down, a Conditional Access misconfiguration has locked every admin out, or a ransomware incident demands immediate top-level control? That is the job of a small number of break-glass accounts held in reserve — the documented exception to your own guardrails.

Because these accounts bypass the usual controls, the entire control set is detection over prevention. You cannot rely on the fence, so you rely on making every use impossible to hide and impossible to ignore:

Sealed — the credential is split into parts held by different custodians (a physical safe or a tightly controlled vault entry) so no single person can wield it alone. This multi-person (M-of-N) control stops one insider or one stolen credential half.
Monitored — any invocation fires loud, hard-to-suppress real-time alerts to security and leadership. A break-glass account signing in on a normal Tuesday is itself an incident.
Rehearsed — the procedure is tested and recertified periodically. A sealed account nobody can actually open in a crisis is worse than useless.

Two rules make or break it. Exclude these accounts from the very control that could lock them out (e.g. exempt them from the Conditional Access policy that failed) — but monitor them the hardest. And after every use, run the mandatory review: rotate the secret, re-split, re-seal, and file the record. An emergency credential still valid after the incident is just an unmonitored superuser password.

lessons.title: PAM vaulting and session recording
lessons.objective: See how a vault removes direct credential handling and how a session proxy makes shared-account activity attributable.
lessons.content:
JIT elevates a role on your own identity. But some privileges are a shared secret — a local-admin password, a database sa account, an appliance root — that cannot practically be made per-person. The PAM answer is to never let the secret touch the administrator's machine.

Vault check-out / check-in. The credential lives only inside the vault. To use it the admin checks it out: the vault verifies who they are, checks entitlement and any approval, then either reveals the secret for a bounded window or — far better — brokers it by injecting it straight into a session so the human never sees the value at all. On check-in (explicit, on session end, or on timeout) the vault rotates the credential, so what was checked out can never be reused. Prefer brokering over revealing: a secret the human never sees cannot be written down, pasted into chat, or phished later. Bind every check-out to a specific human so the log answers "who used root at 02:00", not just "root logged in".

Session recording and monitoring. The brokered connection is routed through an inline session proxy (a Privileged Session Manager) that injects the target credential, records the session — screen capture plus a structured keystroke/command log — and runs a real-time policy engine per command. A prohibited command can be blocked in-line; a hard-rule violation or a live reviewer can terminate the session mid-stream. Recordings go to append-only / WORM storage with integrity hashing, because a log an admin can edit is not audit evidence. And the proxy fails closed: if the recorder or policy engine is down, deny new privileged sessions rather than allow an unrecorded one.

lessons.title: Continuous and adaptive access
lessons.objective: Move the check from login-time to session-time: CAE near-real-time revocation, device posture, and the MFA-fatigue problem.
lessons.content:
Everything so far minimizes standing privilege. Adaptive access attacks the other assumption: that a decision made at login stays valid for the life of the session. It does not.

Continuous Access Evaluation (CAE). A bearer token is honoured until it expires — so a one-hour token stays valid for up to an hour even if the user is disabled, the password is reset, or the session is flagged risky the moment after issuance. CAE closes that gap by keeping the resource server and IdP talking after issuance. On a critical event (account disabled, password reset, MFA revoked, admin sign-out, elevated risk, network-location change) the next API call is met with a claims challenge (WWW-Authenticate with a claims parameter) instead of being served; the client takes that back to the IdP, which re-evaluates and re-issues or blocks. Enforcement moves from token-expiry to near-real-time — it shrinks the window, it does not eliminate it, so pair it with short lifetimes for the most sensitive resources.

Device posture. A valid identity is necessary but not sufficient; the request must also come from a compliant, managed device. The policy engine requires a device certificate or hardware attestation, then checks posture (encrypted, patched, EDR healthy, not jailbroken) and maps it to grant / limited / block. Do not trust client-asserted posture — root it in hardware attestation (TPM, Secure Enclave). And compliance is a snapshot: pair it with CAE so posture drift revokes access mid-session, not only at the next login.

The MFA-fatigue problem. Push-based MFA has a specific weakness: an attacker who already holds the password sprays approve/deny prompts until a worn-down user taps Approve ("push bombing"). Number matching defeats it — the sign-in screen shows a two- or three-digit number the user must type into the app. The number lives on the initiator's screen, which during an attack is the attacker's, so the victim has no correct number to enter. It stops blind approval, but not a real-time AiTM relay — for that, move to phishing-resistant FIDO2 / passkeys. And treat unrequested prompts as signal: a burst the user never started means the password has already fallen.

quiz.q: Under just-in-time elevation, what does an "eligible" assignment grant before activation?
choices: Full use of the privileged role at all times
Nothing on its own — the privilege is dormant until it is activated
A permanent role that is merely hidden from audit
Standing access limited to business hours
quiz.explain: Eligibility is not access. The standing state is unprivileged; the role is conferred only on activation (justification + fresh MFA, possibly approval) and is auto-revoked when the time-bound window ends.

quiz.q: Why is a fresh, phishing-resistant MFA challenge required at the moment of activation, not just a valid existing session?
choices: Because sessions cannot carry MFA claims
Because activation is the moment privilege is actually conferred, so it deserves the strongest proof
To reset the session cookie
Because approvers cannot see session state
quiz.explain: A valid sign-in session is not enough: activation is when standing-zero privilege becomes real access, so it is re-authenticated with a fresh phishing-resistant factor rather than trusting an earlier login.

quiz.q: Break-glass emergency accounts bypass the usual guardrails. What is the primary control model that keeps them safe?
choices: Prevention — tight network firewalls block their use
Detection and accountability — loud alerting, logging, multi-person control, and mandatory post-use review
Short-lived tokens that expire in minutes
Automatic role revocation after each API call
quiz.explain: Because these accounts exist precisely to bypass controls, the guarantees come from detection over prevention: seal the credential under multi-person control, raise hard-to-suppress alerts on any use, and mandatorily reseal and rotate afterward.

quiz.q: In the strongest credential-vault model, how does the administrator use a shared privileged password?
choices: The vault emails the password for offline storage
The vault brokers it — injecting the secret into the session so the human never sees the value, then rotating on check-in
The password is copied permanently to the admin's workstation
The admin memorizes the password so it need not be rotated
quiz.explain: Brokering is preferred over revealing: a secret the human never sees cannot be written down, pasted into chat, or phished later. The vault rotates the credential on check-in so the checked-out value can never be reused.

quiz.q: Number matching stops push-bombing but does NOT stop which attack?
choices: A user tapping Approve out of fatigue
An attacker with only the victim's password spraying prompts
A real-time adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) proxy that relays a legitimate challenge
A guessed or mistyped number on the authenticator
quiz.explain: Number matching defeats blind approval because the number lives on the initiator's (attacker's) screen. It does not stop an AiTM proxy relaying a genuine challenge in real time — that requires phishing-resistant FIDO2 / passkeys.

stages.title: Threats & defense
stages.summary: Five identity attacks that beat passwords and even MFA — AiTM phishing, token replay, Golden SAML, Kerberoasting, and consent/device-code phishing — each paired with the control that actually stops it.

lessons.title: Adversary-in-the-middle MFA phishing
lessons.objective: See why reverse-proxy phishing defeats OTP and push, and why passkeys break it.
lessons.content:
The attack. Adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) phishing defeats most multi-factor authentication by proxying the real login instead of harvesting a static password. The attacker stands up a reverse-proxy phishing site that relays every request and response between the victim and the legitimate IdP in real time. The victim sees the genuine login and MFA challenge — because it is genuine, relayed through the proxy — completes MFA, and the IdP issues a session cookie or token. Because that cookie flows back through the proxy, the attacker captures it and replays the authenticated session. No password or second factor is needed thereafter. OTP, push, and SMS all fall the same way: the proxy simply relays the one-time value, so the second factor adds no friction.

The defense. The durable fix is phishing-resistant FIDO2 / passkeys. A passkey signs over the real origin, and the IdP checks it; an assertion produced against the proxy's look-alike origin will not validate, so the login never completes — origin binding is what actually breaks AiTM. Layer on sender-constrained sessions (token binding, DPoP, mTLS) so a captured cookie cannot be replayed from another host, continuous access evaluation and short session lifetimes to evict a replayed session fast on risk signals, and conditional access requiring compliant/managed devices — which the attacker's replay host is not.

lessons.title: Token theft and replay
lessons.objective: Understand how stolen bearer tokens are replayed, and how to make tokens non-portable.
lessons.content:
The attack. A bearer token grants access to whoever presents it, so an attacker who lifts an access or refresh token — from browser storage, logs, a memory dump, an infostealer, or a compromised proxy — can replay it against the API or redeem a stolen refresh token for fresh access tokens, impersonating the victim with no password or MFA prompt. A long-lived refresh token is especially valuable: it can be redeemed repeatedly and often outlives a password reset, giving durable persistence. This is frequently the payoff stage of AiTM or consent phishing, which produce the very tokens replayed here.

The defense. Make the token non-bearer by sender-constraining it: DPoP (a proof-of-possession JWT) or mutual-TLS certificate binding ties the token to a client key, so a copy replayed from another host lacks the private key and is rejected. Pair that with refresh-token rotation and reuse detection — each refresh returns a new token and invalidates the old one, so a replayed refresh token trips a tripwire and the IdP revokes the entire token family. Add continuous access evaluation (CAE) and short access-token lifetimes to invalidate stolen tokens mid-lifetime, and protect tokens at rest by keeping them out of localStorage and logs.

lessons.title: Golden SAML
lessons.objective: Learn how a stolen IdP signing key forges assertions, and why key custody is the control.
lessons.content:
The attack. Golden SAML is a forgery against SAML federation. An attacker who steals the Identity Provider's token-signing private key (and its certificate) can mint arbitrarily valid SAML assertions for any user, with any groups or attributes, without ever authenticating at the IdP. Because the Service Provider trusts anything signed by that key, a forged assertion is indistinguishable from a real one — and it bypasses the MFA and conditional access that live at the IdP. It is a post-compromise move: the attacker must already have exported the key from a soft key store, a backup, or the federation config database, and can then persist even after passwords are reset, since the signing key is the secret.

The defense. This is fundamentally a key-management problem — once the key leaks, the SP cannot cryptographically tell a forgery from the genuine article. The primary control is to hold the signing key in an HSM (or a KMS with non-exportable keys) so it cannot be stolen and reused offline, and to harden the federation server as a Tier-0 asset. For detection, correlate SP logins with IdP authentication events: a golden assertion produces a successful SP session with no matching IdP sign-in, the single strongest signal. Rotate the signing key on a schedule and after any suspected compromise, enforce short assertion lifetimes with strict NotOnOrAfter and audience validation, and watch for unexpected signing certificates added to SP trust.

lessons.title: Kerberoasting
lessons.objective: Grasp offline cracking of service tickets and why strong or managed passwords defeat it.
lessons.content:
The attack. Kerberoasting abuses a normal feature of the Kerberos TGS exchange: any authenticated domain user can request a service ticket for any account that has a Service Principal Name (SPN) registered. Part of that ticket is encrypted with a key derived from the service account's password. The attacker requests the ticket, extracts the encrypted portion, and cracks the password offline — with no further traffic to the KDC and no failed-logon noise. A single low-privileged foothold is enough to roast every SPN in the domain, and accounts with weak, human-chosen passwords and legacy RC4 encryption fall quickly, especially over-privileged SQL, IIS, and legacy-app accounts.

The defense. Kerberoasting cannot be blocked at the protocol level — issuing service tickets is the KDC's job — so the goal is to make the cracked material worthless and the request pattern visible. The top control is group Managed Service Accounts (gMSA/dMSA) or 25+ character random passwords: a 120-character auto-rotated secret makes offline cracking computationally infeasible. Enforce AES and remove RC4 so tickets are far more expensive to crack, practice SPN hygiene and least privilege so no service account sits in Tier-0 groups, and monitor Windows event 4769 for a single account requesting many distinct SPNs or RC4 tickets. A honeypot SPN with no legitimate use turns any request for it into a high-fidelity alert.

lessons.title: Consent and device-code phishing
lessons.objective: Recognize illicit OAuth grants and the governance controls that block or contain them.
lessons.content:
The attack. Both techniques abuse legitimate OAuth flows without ever stealing a password. In consent phishing (the illicit consent grant), the attacker registers or impersonates a malicious app and lures the victim to a genuine IdP consent screen; when the victim clicks Accept, the IdP issues the attacker's app real access and refresh tokens for scopes like mail, files, and offline_access. In device-code phishing, the attacker starts the OAuth device grant on their own machine, obtains a valid user_code, and phishes the victim to enter it at the real verification URL; on approval, tokens land in the attacker's polling client. Both survive password resets and bypass MFA — MFA is satisfied during the victim's own login — and device-code phishing needs no fake page at all, since the victim only ever touches the legitimate IdP.

The defense. These are authorization problems, not authentication ones — the crypto and login are valid — so defense centers on governing which apps and grants are permitted. Restrict user consent to verified publishers and a low-risk scope allowlist, and route everything else through an admin consent workflow with human review; require publisher verification so unverified apps never reach a grantable screen. For the device grant, use conditional access to restrict or disable it to compliant/managed devices, enforce short user_code lifetimes and polling slow-down, and show a clear approval screen that names the app and asks "did you start this?". Back both with app-governance / risky-app detection that can revoke a grant and its refresh tokens after the fact, plus least-privilege scopes and periodic access reviews.

quiz.q: A user completes a push-approval MFA prompt on a real-looking login page, yet the attacker gains an authenticated session. What made this possible?
choices: The attacker guessed the one-time code
A reverse proxy relayed the genuine login and captured the issued session cookie
The user's password was weak
MFA was disabled for the account
quiz.explain: In AiTM phishing the attacker proxies the real IdP, so the victim's genuine MFA succeeds and the resulting session cookie flows back through the proxy to be replayed. The second factor adds no friction because it is simply relayed.

quiz.q: Which control most directly prevents AiTM phishing from completing the login at all?
choices: SMS one-time passwords
Longer password requirements
Origin-bound FIDO2 / passkeys
A CAPTCHA on the login page
quiz.explain: A passkey signs over the real origin and the IdP verifies it, so an assertion produced against the proxy's look-alike origin fails validation. Origin binding stops the login rather than merely containing a stolen session.

quiz.q: An attacker presents a previously-rotated refresh token to the IdP. In a well-configured system, what should happen?
choices: The IdP silently issues a new access token
Nothing — refresh tokens never expire
The IdP detects reuse and revokes the entire token family
The API validates only the signature and allows it
quiz.explain: Refresh-token rotation with reuse detection makes each refresh single-use; presenting an already-used token is a high-fidelity signal that a stolen copy is in play, so the whole token family is revoked.

quiz.q: What is the single strongest detection signal for a Golden SAML forgery?
choices: A spike in failed password attempts at the IdP
A successful SP session with no corresponding IdP authentication event
An expired signing certificate
A high volume of Kerberos event 4769
quiz.explain: A forged assertion is signed with the stolen key and never touches the IdP's login, so it produces an SP sign-in with no matching IdP authentication. Correlating SP and IdP logs surfaces exactly that mismatch.

quiz.q: Why is a group Managed Service Account (gMSA) the top control against Kerberoasting?
choices: It blocks the KDC from ever issuing service tickets
It forces all logins through MFA
It gives the account a long, random, auto-rotated password that is infeasible to crack offline
It removes the account's SPN automatically
quiz.explain: Kerberoasting relies on cracking the service account's password offline. A gMSA uses a 120+ character randomly generated secret rotated automatically, so the extracted ciphertext is not practically crackable — the attack is neutralized even though tickets are still issued.

stages.title: Architecture, CI/CD & Delivery
stages.summary: The capstone: how the pieces assemble into a real system. Inside a modern IdP, how enterprise identity products fit together, how zero trust decides every request, and how you ship and stand up all of it — keyless deploys, signed artifacts, and environments as code.

lessons.title: Inside an identity provider
lessons.objective: See the components a modern IdP is built from and the trust boundaries between them.
lessons.content:
Everything you have learned about login flows runs through a system: the Identity Provider. Seen from the inside, an IdP is not one box but a set of cooperating planes, each with a different job and a different level of exposure:

  • Edge / TLS gateway — the only internet-facing component. TLS terminates here; a WAF and rate limiter blunt credential stuffing and DoS before traffic reaches anything sensitive.
  • Authentication service — runs the login ceremony, verifies primary credentials, and orchestrates factors via the Factor / MFA service (TOTP, push, WebAuthn/passkey).
  • Token / assertion service — mints OIDC ID/access tokens (JWT) and SAML assertions. It signs with private keys held in an HSM/KMS, the crown jewels — keys never leave the boundary, and the public half is published via JWKS or SAML metadata.
  • Session store — the IdP's own long-lived, revocable SSO session, distinct from the short-lived tokens it mints for relying parties.
  • User directory — the authoritative store of identities, credential hashes, and group membership; the highest-value data store, isolated in the data tier.
  • Policy/admin plane and append-only audit log — management flows through its own MFA-protected, audited path, and every authN, token issuance, and admin action is written to a tamper-evident log.

The point of drawing these boundaries is containment: only the edge is public, only the token service touches signing keys, and a compromise in one plane does not automatically grant the others.

lessons.title: A real enterprise identity environment
lessons.objective: Place SailPoint, Okta/Entra, Active Directory, and applications in one picture.
lessons.content:
A single IdP is only part of the estate. In a real enterprise, several systems each own a distinct role and hand off to the next:

  • HR system of record (e.g. Workday) — authoritative worker data; a hire, transfer, or termination here triggers the joiner/mover/leaver lifecycle.
  • Identity governance / IGA (e.g. SailPoint) — the control plane. It provisions accounts, runs access requests and certifications, and enforces separation of duties.
  • Access management / IdP (e.g. Okta, Microsoft Entra ID) — run-time authentication, MFA, and SSO into applications.
  • Directory (e.g. Active Directory) — on-prem accounts, groups, and Kerberos/LDAP.
  • Privileged access / PAM (e.g. CyberArk) — vaulted credentials and brokered privileged sessions.
  • Applications — the relying parties that consume SSO and provisioned access.

The shape is what matters, and product names are interchangeable: an HR source of truth feeds an IGA control plane that provisions a directory, an IdP, and apps, while the IdP handles authentication and SSO at run time and a PAM tool brokers privileged access. Governance decides who should have access; the IdP enforces who is present right now.

lessons.title: Zero trust: decide every request
lessons.objective: Understand the PDP/PEP split, continuous verification, and why network location grants nothing.
lessons.content:
Zero trust (NIST SP 800-207) replaces the old "inside the perimeter is trusted" model with a rule: every request to every resource is mediated and re-verified. Two roles do the work:

Policy Decision Point (PDP) — the brain, made of a Policy Engine that computes the allow/deny decision from policy plus signals, and a Policy Administrator that establishes or tears down the connection and issues session credentials.

Policy Enforcement Point (PEP) — the inline gate sitting in front of each resource. It allows, blocks, or terminates a session on the PDP's instruction. An API gateway is a concrete PEP.

The decision is a function of live signals, not a one-time login: identity and MFA from the IdP, device posture from EDR, and risk from SIEM/threat intel are combined per request. Key consequences:

  • No network-location trust — internal traffic is challenged exactly like internet traffic. This is the model that replaces IP-allowlist "network auth".
  • Continuous verification — sessions are short and re-evaluated; a device that falls out of compliance mid-session is denied on the next check, and the PA can revoke an established session when a signal changes.
  • Least privilege, per-resource — access is to a single resource for a single session, so lateral movement is denied by default.
  • Control plane vs data plane — the PDP never carries application data, so compromising the data path does not grant policy authority. But the PDP and its signal feeds are high-value: poisoned posture or risk data corrupts every decision.

lessons.title: Secure delivery: keyless deploys and provenance
lessons.objective: Ship without stored cloud keys and refuse artifacts that cannot prove where they came from.
lessons.content:
The same identity principles apply to how software reaches production. Two patterns remove long-lived secrets from the pipeline.

OIDC-to-cloud federation (keyless deploy). Instead of pasting a long-lived cloud access key into CI secrets, the CI system acts as an OIDC issuer: for each job it mints a short-lived, signed JWT describing the workflow — claims like sub=repo:org/repo:ref:refs/heads/main, aud, and environment. The cloud is configured to trust that issuer and exchanges the JWT for short-lived credentials (AWS sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity, GCP Workload Identity Federation, Azure workload identity federation). The exchange succeeds only if the signature verifies against the issuer's JWKS and the claims satisfy the trust policy. The cardinal rule: scope sub and aud tightly and never wildcard the subject — a loose repo:org/* lets a fork assume your role.

Artifact signing and provenance (verify on deploy). Prove an artifact was built by a trusted pipeline from trusted source, and refuse anything that cannot. With Sigstore keyless signing, cosign gets an OIDC identity token, Fulcio issues a short-lived cert bound to that identity, cosign signs the artifact digest, and the signature is recorded in the Rekor transparency log — no signing key is stored. The build also emits signed in-toto provenance (source, builder, materials), graded by SLSA level. At deploy, an admission controller or deploy gate verifies the signer identity (not just that a signature exists), checks the provenance meets the required SLSA level and builder, and only then admits the artifact. Verify at admission, not only at build.

lessons.title: Environments as code, and where to go next
lessons.objective: Stand up Okta/Auth0/SailPoint/Entra/AD from reviewed, versioned templates — then keep exploring.
lessons.content:
The identity platforms themselves can be declared and deployed like any other infrastructure. The environment templates are copyable, parameterized starters — one per platform, each with a GitHub Actions workflow:

  • Okta (Workforce) and Auth0 (CIAM) — Terraform providers.
  • SailPoint ISC — SP-Config JSON driven by the SailPoint CLI/API.
  • Microsoft Entra ID — the azuread Terraform provider.
  • Active Directory — a PowerShell baseline for OUs, groups, and tiering.

The shared conventions turn these into a safe workflow: multi-environment (dev/test/prod, never one shared state), remote state, secrets never in code (only *.tfvars.example is committed; real values come from CI secrets or, better, OIDC federation), least privilege per-environment service principals, and plan on PR, apply on merge gated by a protected production environment with manual approval. They are starter templates, not turn-key production configs — always read a plan before applying to a real tenant.

Where to go next. You now have the whole picture: identity vocabulary, login and token flows, authorization, lifecycle, and how it all assembles and ships. When you face a real choice, reach for the decision guides — which authentication protocol, session vs. token, authorization model, MFA factor, OAuth grant, or workload-to-cloud auth. And to watch any flow run message by message, open the interactive Flow Explorer. Build the mental model here; make the call there.

quiz.q: In the IdP reference architecture, which component holds the private keys used to sign tokens and assertions?
choices: The Edge / TLS gateway
The Token / assertion service, backed by an HSM/KMS
The user directory
The session store
quiz.explain: The token/assertion service signs with private keys held in an HSM/KMS. Those keys are the crown jewels — they never leave the boundary, and only the public half is published via JWKS or SAML metadata.

quiz.q: In a typical enterprise identity environment, which system is the authoritative source that triggers the joiner/mover/leaver lifecycle?
choices: The IdP (Okta / Entra ID)
Active Directory
The HR system of record (e.g. Workday)
The PAM tool (e.g. CyberArk)
quiz.explain: The HR system of record holds authoritative worker data; a hire, transfer, or termination there triggers the lifecycle, which the IGA control plane then provisions into the directory, IdP, and apps.

quiz.q: A laptop passes login and starts a session, then falls out of patch compliance an hour later. What does a zero-trust architecture do?
choices: Nothing — it was already trusted at login for the life of the session
Denies it on the next evaluation, because decisions combine live signals per request and sessions are continuously re-verified
Trusts it as long as it stays on the internal network
Re-runs MFA but keeps network access regardless of posture
quiz.explain: Zero trust makes each decision a function of live signals (identity, device posture, risk), not a one-time login. A device that falls out of compliance is denied on the next check, and the Policy Administrator can revoke an established session.

quiz.q: What is the single most important condition to get right in an OIDC-to-cloud trust policy for keyless deploys?
choices: Give the credentials a long TTL so jobs never expire mid-run
Store a backup access key in CI secrets in case OIDC fails
Scope the subject and audience tightly and never wildcard the subject
Allow any valid signature from the CI issuer
quiz.explain: The exchange must require a tightly scoped sub and aud. A wildcard subject like repo:org/* lets a fork or unrelated repo assume the role, undoing the whole model. Pin to a ref or, better, an environment claim.

quiz.q: With keyless artifact signing (Sigstore), how should a deploy gate decide whether to admit an image?
choices: Admit any image that carries some signature
Verify at build time only; admission does not need to re-check
Verify the signer identity (OIDC issuer/subject) and that provenance meets the required SLSA level and builder, at admission
Require a long-lived signing key to be stored and rotated
quiz.explain: Verify the signer identity, not merely the presence of a signature, and require trusted-builder provenance at a minimum SLSA level. Do this at admission, since build-time checks do not stop a tampered artifact from being deployed by another path.
